parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: e.m.f. as energy per unit charge
terminal p.d. as energy delivered to external circuit
hints: Hint 1: Think about where the energy supplied by the battery per unit charge ends up when there is both an external resistor and resistance inside the battery itself.
parts.proper_answer: Some of the energy supplied by the battery is dissipated as heat in the internal resistance $r$, so less energy per unit charge is available to the external resistor and $V < E$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What E and V really mean**
Think of $E$ as the total electrical energy the battery gives to each coulomb of charge that passes through it. Think of $V$ as the energy each coulomb actually delivers to the outside resistor $R$.

Step 2: **Where the missing energy goes**
The charge also has to flow through the material of the battery itself, which has internal resistance $r$. Work is done against $r$ and energy is dissipated as heat inside the battery. So $$V = E - \text{energy lost per unit charge in } r$$ and therefore $V$ is less than $E$ whenever current flows.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Remember that the total e.m.f. is shared between the external resistor and the inside of the battery, and consider what the p.d. across the internal resistance depends on.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Splitting up the e.m.f.**
The e.m.f. $E$ drives current $I$ round the whole loop. Part of it appears across the external resistor as $V$, and part is lost across the internal resistance.

Step 2: **Lost volts**
By Ohm's law, the p.d. across the internal resistance is $Ir$. Adding the two parts gives $$E = V + Ir$$ which can also be written $V = E - Ir$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the left-hand end of the line in Fig. 6.2 and think about what physical situation $I = 0$ corresponds to for the external circuit.
parts.proper_answer: When $I = 0$ there is no p.d. lost across the internal resistance, so $V = E$. The intercept on the $V$-axis in Fig. 6.2 is $2.8\text{ V}$, so $E = 2.8\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading the intercept**
In Fig. 6.2 the straight line meets the $V$-axis at $2.8\text{ V}$ when $I = 0$. Extrapolate the line back carefully to $I = 0$ to see this maximum value.

Step 2: **Why intercept equals E**
From $V = E - Ir$, if $I = 0$ then $Ir = 0$ and $$V = E$$ This is the open-circuit case where no current flows and no energy is lost inside the battery. So the $V$-intercept directly gives $E = 2.8\text{ V}$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how $V$ changes with $I$ in $V = E - Ir$ and think about what feature of a straight-line $V$ against $I$ graph tells you about $r$.
Hint 2: Pick two widely spaced points on the line in Fig. 6.2, for example the intercept and the point at $I = 1.0\text{ A}$, and use the change in $V$ divided by the change in $I$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Gradient gives r**
Rewrite the equation as $$V = E - Ir$$ This is of the form $y = c + mx$ with gradient $-r$. So the magnitude of the gradient of the $V$ against $I$ graph equals $r$.

Step 2: **Calculate from the graph**
Take e.g. $V = 2.8\text{ V}$ at $I = 0$ and $V = 1.4\text{ V}$ at $I = 1.0\text{ A}$: $$r = -\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I} = -\frac{1.4 - 2.8}{1.0 - 0} = 1.4\,\Omega$$ Any other pair of points on the line gives the same result, about $1.4\,\Omega$.

parts.label: (d)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding from Fig. 6.2 the current that flows when the terminal p.d. is $2.1\text{ V}$, then think about how $V$, $I$ and $R$ are linked for the external resistor alone.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the current**
On Fig. 6.2, draw across from $V = 2.1\text{ V}$ to the line and down to the $I$-axis. You get $$I = 0.50\text{ A}$$

Step 2: **Apply Ohm's law to R**
For the external resistor alone, $$R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{2.1}{0.50} = 4.2\,\Omega$$

parts.label: (d)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how much total charge passes in $1.0\text{ s}$ at a current of $0.50\text{ A}$, and how that charge is built up from individual electron charges.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Charge in 1.0 s**
Current is rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$. With $I = 0.50\text{ A}$ and $t = 1.0\text{ s}$: $$Q = It = 0.50 \times 1.0 = 0.50\text{ C}$$

Step 2: **Convert to electrons**
Each electron carries $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$. So $$n = \frac{Q}{e} = \frac{0.50}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.1 \times 10^{18}$$

parts.label: (d)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Start by working out how much stored energy has actually been used up when the store falls from $9.2\text{ kJ}$ to $1.6\text{ kJ}$.
Hint 2: Think about which e.m.f. and current control the total rate at which the battery supplies energy, not just the energy delivered externally.
Hint 3: Link the energy used to $E$, $I$ and time $t$ and rearrange to find $t$, remembering to convert kJ to J.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy delivered by battery**
Energy used $=$ initial store $-$ final store: $$\Delta W = (9.2 - 1.6) \times 10^{3} = 7.6 \times 10^{3}\text{ J}$$

Step 2: **Relate to E, I and t**
The total power supplied by the e.m.f. is $P = EI$, so total energy supplied in time $t$ is $$W = EIt$$ Here $E = 2.8\text{ V}$ and $I = 0.50\text{ A}$ remain constant.

Step 3: **Solve for time**
$$7.6 \times 10^{3} = 2.8 \times 0.50 \times t$$ $$t = \frac{7.6 \times 10^{3}}{1.4} = 5.4 \times 10^{3}\text{ s}$$ This is about 1.5 hours.
